newsitem.title: USA: Wells Fargo misplaces deposits in First Interstate integration.
newsitem.headline: Wells Fargo misplaces deposits in First Interstate integration.

text.p: Misplaced customer deposits and further headaches arising from the integration of First Interstate Bancorp cost Wells Fargo and Co. about $150 million in the second quarter, the bank said Tuesday.
San Francisco-based Wells Fargo reported net income fell to $228 million, or $2.49 a share, in the quarter, from $363 million, or $3.61 a share, a year earlier.

Wells Fargo, which has faced substantial customer slippage since completion of the $11 billion hostile merger last year, said discrepancies in the clearing of accounts with other banks and incorrect posting of deposits caused about $150 million in operating losses for the second quarter.
Another $30 million in operating losses related to more typical problems that occur with credit card and checking accounts, the bank said.
Earnings were close to forecasts of $2.52 a share after the bank said last week that profits would suffer because of troubles integrating First Interstate.
"The results were not much worse than they warned. They were basically in the range," Stephen Biggar at S&P Equity Group said.
Wells Fargo stock rose $1.50 to $267 on the New York Stock Exchange, recovering some of its 6.6 percent drop after its earnings warning last Wednesday.
One analyst said the troubles were because it was not a friendly merger.

"I have a feeling it has a lot to with the the fact it was a hostile merger. A lot of top managers left Interstate when the deal closed. At this stage, you have to wonder if it would have gone a lot more smoothly had they stuck around," the analyst said.
On a conference call, Wells Fargo Chief Financial Officer Rod Jacobs said there was no doubt the loss of key Interstate managers played a role.
However, he said, "I think the bulk of the problems generated through the integration were by our own making.
"The integration schedule ended up being too fast and as a result, some things got broken. We probably had too much confidence as miracle workers and we didn't do it this time," he said.

Jacobs said the customer account runoff for Wells Fargo outside of California, where about 30 percent of its deposits are located, has averaged about 1.5 percent in the first two quarters of 1997, with mimimal growth in California accounts.

Wells Chairman Paul Hazen said he was disappointed with the second-quarter results, but Jacobs said the losses resulted from the cleanup of old problems that arose between November and February. He said the bank expects a more normal level of operating losses moving forward as the integration proceeds "We do not anticipate any more unusual items," Jacobs said.
He said the largest component of the $150 million in operating losses related to discrepancies at its clearing unit's account of money flows between its affiliates and the Federal Reserve.

"This unit got swamped during the conversion, and we found some assets on the balance sheet where we couldn't justify the carrying value. There's some chance we might have claims against other banks," Jacobs said.

The rest of the losses related to the incorrect posting of some customer deposits several months ago in which deposits never made it to the accounts. Wells Fargo credited the customers but was unable in some cases to find the deposits and had to write them off.
As far as the retrieval of the lost deposits, Jacobs said few customers have reported a windfall of unexplained funds.

"We have a few customers who have pointed out errors ... but we don't have a long list of customers who have indicated we've put too much money in their account or paid too much on their loan," he said.
Jacobs rejected claims by industry sources and analysts that competitors, such as Glendale Federal Bank, Sanwa Bank Ltd. and BankAmerica Corp. have benefited from its customer declines.
